title: Hosting and Deploying MCP Servers
description: Deploy MCP servers in ASP.NET Core, secure remote access, and manage secrets and configuration for production.

blocks.text: Production MCP servers need the same operational rigor as any backend service: secrets management, HTTPS, health checks, scaling, and monitoring. ASP.NET Core provides all of these primitives.

blocks.title: Hosting choices
items: **ASP.NET Core minimal API** — expose MCP over HTTP with standard middleware.
**Background worker** — run MCP server as a hosted service inside an existing app.
**Container deployment** — package the server for Kubernetes or container apps.
**Serverless function** — possible for lightweight tools, but cold start can hurt UX.

blocks.title: Conceptual ASP.NET Core MCP endpoint
Use standard hosting patterns
blocks.text: Do not invent custom hosting logic for MCP. Use ASP.NET Core features for configuration, logging, health checks, and secret management.

items.text: My MCP server runs over HTTPS in production
items.hint: Use HSTS, certificate validation, and secure headers

items.text: I manage secrets with configuration providers
items.hint: User secrets in development; environment variables or Key Vault in production

items.text: I expose health and readiness checks
items.hint: Standardize health endpoints for orchestration and monitoring

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: MCP servers can be hosted in standard ASP.NET Core apps.
Production deployments require HTTPS, secrets management, and monitoring.
Container or PaaS hosting works well for scalable MCP services.
blocks.takeaway: Deploy MCP servers with the same rigor as any public API. The protocol is new, but the infrastructure patterns are not.
